blocks.text: Photographer and filmmaker Neal Slavin returns to his alma mater for a conversation with artist and author M. Leona Godin . Their conversation will explore perception and what it truly means to see.

Neal Slavin met M. Leona Godin at the New York Public Library, where Godin was the 2025–26 Jean Strouse Fellow in the Cullman Center for Scholars and Writers. As a fellow, Godin was working on a book about blindness, photography, and image description. Their first encounter sparked many long conversations on the ways perception shapes how we experience the world through photography.

This evening’s conversation will explore the phenomenon of synesthesia, where the boundaries among the senses dissolve and the languages of music, poetry, painting, and photography intermingle. Together, they will discuss how perception moves beyond eyesight alone, and how photography continues to expand our understanding of what it means to see.

Slavin’s portraits have been published in several books, including Portugal , Britons , and When Two or More Are Gathered Together , recently republished and expanded with new photographs that bring together portraits taken over a span of 50 years (1974–2023). He was the recipient of a Fulbright Fellowship in Photography and of Cooper Union’s highest honor, the President’s Citation. Slavin’s photographs are in numerous permanent collections, including The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Centre Pompidou, and the New York Public Library, where Godin first encountered his work.

M. Leona Godin is a blind writer, artist, and the author of There Plant Eyes: A Personal and Cultural History of Blindness . She is currently working on a project about photography, blindness, and what it means to see, which received recent support from an NYPL Cullman Center Fellowship.
